body.p: With every ordinary verb form (present, past, future, subjunctive, perfect), the weak pronoun goes **immediately before the verb**.
Nothing can come between the pronoun and the verb except other weak pronouns. The little words **θα, να, ας, δεν, μην** go **before** the pronoun:
In the perfect tenses the pronoun goes before **έχω**: **Το έχω δει** "I have seen it", **Σας είχαμε γράψει** "We had written to you".

check.why: δεν, then the pronoun, then the verb.
θα always comes before the weak pronoun.
In the perfect, the pronoun goes before έχω.
θα + σε + verb.

sections.el: Μετά την προστακτική και τη μετοχή
sections.title: After commands and the gerund

body.p: There are only two forms after which the weak pronoun **follows** the verb: the **imperative** and the **gerund** (-οντας/-ώντας).
A negative command is not an imperative but **μην + subjunctive**, so the pronoun goes back before the verb: **Πες το!** "Say it!" but **Μην το πεις!** "Don't say it!"

head: Positive
Negative
rows: Μη μου γράψεις. "Don't write to me."

body.p: The polite or soft command with **να** behaves like any subjunctive: **Να μου γράψεις!** "Do write to me!"

check.why: After an imperative the pronoun follows; "tell someone" takes the genitive του.
Negative commands use μην + subjunctive, with the pronoun before the verb.
The pronoun follows the imperative; φέρε often elides to φέρ'.
μην + το + subjunctive φέρεις. Μην keeps its ν before τ.

body.p: When a verb has two weak pronouns, the **genitive** (indirect object, "to whom") comes **first**, the **accusative** (direct object, "what") second. This holds before and after the verb.

head: Before the verb
After an imperative
rows: Μου το έδωσε. "He gave it to me."
Δώσε μου το. "Give it to me."
Θα του το στείλω. "I'll send it to him."
Στείλ' του το. "Send it to him."
Μην της το πεις. "Don't tell her."

body.p: The accusative pair partner is almost always a third person: **το, τα, τον, την, τους, τις**. "He introduced me to her" is not ***μου με σύστησε** but **Με σύστησε σ' αυτήν** (strong pronoun with σε).

body.tip: After the imperative, colloquial Greek also says **Δώσ' το μου** with the accusative first. Both orders are heard; **δώσε μου το** is the safe one to use.

check.why: Genitive first, accusative second, both before the verb.
After the imperative: genitive then accusative.
θα + genitive + accusative + verb.
μην + του + το + δώσεις.

body.p: A Greek word cannot carry its stress further back than the third syllable from the end. When a weak pronoun is added after a word stressed on its **third-from-last** syllable, or two pronouns are added after a word stressed on its **second-from-last**, the stress would fall too far back, so the word gets a **second accent** on its last syllable.
When the word is stressed on its last two syllables there is no change: **πες μου, δώσε μου, το σπίτι μου, ο φίλος μου**.

body.tip: Without the second accent the clitic can be mistaken for a word of its own: **ο φίλος μου είπε** "my friend said" versus **ο φίλος μού είπε** "the friend told me". Here the accent on μού marks it as belonging to the verb. This is the only time a weak pronoun is written with an accent before the verb.

check.why: διάβασε is stressed on the third syllable from the end, so adding το gives a second accent: διάβασέ το.
Two pronouns after a word stressed on the second-from-last syllable: extra accent on the first pronoun.
Stress on the third-from-last syllable, so a second accent goes on the last syllable.
The gerund is stressed on the third-from-last syllable before the pronoun.

body.p: Greek often uses a weak pronoun **together with** the noun it stands for. This is not a mistake: it marks the noun as a topic (see the word-order guide).

ex.en: Giannis, I've known him for years.
Did you see it, the message?

ex.el: Στη Μαρία της αρέσει το κρασί.

body.p: With **αρέσει, λείπει, φαίνεται** and other verbs whose experiencer is in the genitive, doubling is almost obligatory when the person is a full noun: **Στον Νίκο του αρέσει η θάλασσα** "Nikos likes the sea". Without **του** the sentence sounds incomplete in speech.
With strong pronouns (**εμένα, εσένα, αυτόν**) the weak form is required as well: **Εμένα με ξέχασες** "You forgot *me*", **Σ' εμένα μου το είπε** "He told *me*".

head: Without doubling
With doubling
rows: Στη Μαρία της είπα την αλήθεια.

links.el: Δεξιά μετάθεση: το λέω στο τέλος
links.title: Right dislocation: adding the topic at the end

check.why: A strong pronoun needs its weak form next to the verb.

options: Η μητέρα μου της αρέσει το θέατρο.
Στη μητέρα μου της αρέσει το θέατρο.
Της μητέρας μου αρέσει το θέατρο το.
check.answer: Στη μητέρα μου της αρέσει το θέατρο.
check.why: The experiencer of αρέσει is σε + accusative (or genitive), doubled by της.
Fronted object, then its doubling pronoun before the verb.

sections.el: Αλυσίδες ρημάτων: κάθε αντωνυμία στο ρήμα της
sections.title: Verb chains: each pronoun stays with its own verb

body.p: In a chain such as "I want to see it", the pronoun belongs to the verb whose object it is, and stays **inside** that verb's clause. Greek never moves it up to the first verb, as Italian or Spanish can.

ex.en: I want to see it. (not *Το θέλω να δω)
Can you give it to me?

body.p: If both verbs have an object, each takes its own pronoun: **Τον παρακάλεσα να μου το στείλει** "I asked him to send it to me" (τον belongs to παρακάλεσα, μου το to στείλει).
The same rule holds with **για να, πριν να, χωρίς να**: **Το έκανα για να σε βοηθήσω**, **Έφυγε χωρίς να μας χαιρετήσει**.

check.why: The pronoun belongs to βρω, so it goes after να.

check.q: "I asked him to send it to me."
check.answer: Τον παρακάλεσα να μου το στείλει.
check.why: τον with παρακάλεσα; μου το with στείλει.
The weak pronoun follows να and goes before πούμε.

list: **The old order survives in set phrases and dialects.** Folk songs and fixed phrases sometimes put the pronoun after an ordinary verb (**Δόξα σοι ο Θεός**), and Cypriot Greek still does so in everyday speech (**Είδα τον** "I saw him"). In standard Greek this order is wrong outside the imperative and the gerund.
**Two clitics, both accusative, are impossible.** "He made me a doctor" uses a full noun: **Με έκανε γιατρό**.

**Formal writing avoids doubling** but keeps clitics with the genitive experiencer: **Στους πολίτες δεν τους δόθηκε καμία εξήγηση** sounds journalistic; a report would write **Δεν δόθηκε καμία εξήγηση στους πολίτες**.

**The genitive clitic as a possessive in a verb phrase**: **Μου χάλασε το αυτοκίνητο** "My car broke down (on me)", **Του πέθανε η μάνα του** "His mother died (and he lost her)". The clitic shows the person affected; English adds "on me".
**Ethic genitive in commands and wishes**: **Να μου είσαι καλά!** "Be well (for my sake)!", **Πού μου πας;** "Where are you off to?" This **μου** adds warmth and is typical of affectionate speech.

ex.en: My washing machine broke down on me.

ex.el: Δεν δόθηκε καμία εξήγηση στους πολίτες.
ex.en: No explanation was given to the citizens.

check.q: What does **μου** add in **Μου έκλεψαν το πορτοφόλι**?
options: It means "my" only, so it must be removed.
It shows I am the person affected: "They stole my wallet (from me)".
check.answer: It shows I am the person affected: "They stole my wallet (from me)".
check.why: The genitive clitic marks the person affected by the event, often with no need for "my".

check.q: Which is a formal report's version?
options: Στους πολίτες δεν τους δόθηκε εξήγηση.
Δεν τους δόθηκε στους πολίτες εξήγηση.
check.why: Formal writing prefers the plain order without doubling.

title: Weak pronouns in the sentence
blurb: Where με, σου, τον, το, της go: before the verb, after commands and gerunds, in pairs, with θα, να and δεν, doubling a noun, and the accent they can add.

intro.p: The weak (clitic) pronouns **με, σε, τον, την, το, μας, σας, τους, τις, τα** (accusative) and **μου, σου, του, της, μας, σας, τους** (genitive) are the most frequent words in Greek after the article. They have no stress of their own and must lean on a verb. Their position is fixed by strict rules, which this guide sets out one by one, so that you can produce them without thinking.
